summary: This document defines how to duplicate RTP streams, sending copies separated in time to guard against loss from outages. Recovering after an outage is hard in unicast, and this offers a protection method for real-time media.

eli5.summary: If a call drops a chunk, sending a copy of each chunk later lets the listener fill the gap. This explains how to send those copies.

questions: rtp packet loss protection by duplication
what is temporal redundancy in rtp
what is spatial redundancy in rtp
why not use duplication for congestion
subtitle: How to send two copies of an RTP stream, in time or across paths, without breaking RTP or RTCP rules.

tldr.problem: Outages cause packet loss in real-time media, and recovering from them is hard for unicast and harder for multicast, where many receivers may be hit at once.
tldr.mechanism: The sender duplicates the packets into a separate redundant RTP stream with its own SSRC, either delayed in time over the same path (temporal) or sent over different addresses and paths (spatial). Receivers drop the duplicates.
tldr.outcome: Near-zero-loss delivery with bounded delay and predictable overhead, but only in managed networks with spare capacity, and never as a response to congestion.

today: RFC 7198 is a Proposed Standard from April 2014 and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It builds on RFC 7197 and RFC 7104.

sections.title: Why Duplicate RTP Streams
sections.content:
RTP is widely used for IPTV and other real-time multimedia, often over intra-domain UDP/IP multicast. UDP/IP flows cannot detect loss or retransmit, so recovery is left to RTP and the application. Loss may come from congestion, or from an unplanned outage such as a flapping link, an interface failure, a software bug or a cut fiber.

In a carefully managed network, one way to recover without unbounded delay is to send the packets again in a separate redundant stream. For non-congestive loss, the chance that both copies of a packet are lost is quite small.

Duplication has comparatively high bandwidth overhead, since everything is sent twice, but low processing overhead, and the overhead is very predictable. The RFC says retransmission and Forward Error Correction may suit other cases. It documents how to duplicate without breaking RTP and RTCP, because this had not been documented properly.
sections.eli5: Sending everything twice costs extra, but it is simple and you always know exactly how much extra it costs.

sections.title: Temporal and Spatial Redundancy
sections.content:
Dual streaming means sending two redundant RTP streams of the same content, each able to support playback on its own. Three or more streams are possible but rare, because of the overhead and the small extra protection.

Two streams are routing-plane identical if they have the same IP source and destination addresses (plus transport ports), so they take the same path. They are told apart by different SSRCs. With temporal redundancy, also called time-shifted redundancy or delayed duplication, one stream is delayed against the other so that a loss that hits one copy is unlikely to hit the same packet again. The receiver uses identical sequence numbers to find and suppress duplicates, a process called stream merging or de-duplication.

With spatial redundancy, the streams use different IP headers, perhaps from two source interfaces, and can travel over physically diverse paths. An unrecoverable loss then needs two failures hitting the same packet on both paths. With source-specific multicast, each redundant stream is its own SSM session, and the receiving host must join each one.

The two approaches cover different patterns: temporal redundancy helps with transient loss within the duplication window, while spatial redundancy helps with longer-lasting loss on one of the two paths. Spatial redundancy often recovers with less delay if the path delays are about the same. Packet misordering can still happen in both cases and is handled with sequence numbers.
sections.eli5: Temporal redundancy is saying the same thing twice a moment apart. Spatial redundancy is sending the two copies down two different roads.

sections.title: Requirements for Using This Specification
sections.content:
One of two conditions is currently REQUIRED to hold:

  • The original and duplicate RTP streams, each with its own SSRC, are carried in the same m line. Other RTP streams may share that line.
  • They are carried in separate m lines, and no other RTP stream is listed in either line.

If streams are in separate m lines and either line also holds other RTP streams, duplication grouping is not trivial. More signaling would be needed, and the RFC leaves that to future standardization.
sections.eli5: Keep the original and its copy in a neat arrangement so the listener can tell which belongs with which. Messier arrangements are not covered yet.

sections.title: RTP and RTCP Rules for Duplicates
sections.content:
For temporal redundancy, the main and duplicate streams SHOULD use the same 5-tuple of transport protocol, source and destination addresses, and source and destination ports. Using anything else is NOT RECOMMENDED unless the path is known to be free of NAPT devices, load balancers and other middleboxes, since it could cause spatial redundancy and extra delay. The streams share one RTP session, and the sender MUST choose a different SSRC for the duplicate, following Section 8 of RFC 3550.

For spatial redundancy, the duplicate uses a different source and/or destination address and port pair, which makes it a separate RTP session. SSRCs MUST be chosen randomly and will almost certainly differ. An a=group:DUP or a=ssrc-group:DUP line indicates duplication. Combining both kinds of redundancy uses the same mechanisms from both cases.

RTCP rules are the same in both cases. If RTCP is sent for the main stream, the sender MUST also generate it for the duplicate, as if it were a regular stream. The sender MUST NOT copy the main stream's RTCP packets, and MUST use the same RTCP CNAME for both streams so the receiver can synchronize them. RTP timestamps and sequence numbers MUST be identical in both streams, which makes the timeline mapping trivial. Receivers MUST generate RTCP reports for both streams, treating them as separate.
sections.eli5: The copy gets its own name tag so it is not confused with the original, but both wear the same team badge so the listener knows they go together. The copy is a true twin, with the same numbering.

sections.title: Signaling in SDP
sections.content:
The receiver must know a stream is a duplicate rather than a separate stream to be played in parallel. For temporal redundancy this needs an SDP extension in the offer/answer exchange, and a way to say which stream is the duplicate. The RFC says out-of-band signaling is needed. The duplication-delay attribute comes from RFC 7197 and the grouping semantics from RFC 7104.

In the RFC's temporal example, SSRCs 1000 and 1010 are grouped with a=ssrc-group:DUP 1000 1010 and a=duplication-delay:50 is set. RFC 7104 advises that the SSRC listed first is sent first, but this is not critical. A receiver should size its playout buffer from the duplication-delay value and play whichever stream arrives first, using the other as a repair stream, whatever order they were signaled in.

The spatial example uses a=group:DUP S1a S1b with two m lines, each with its own multicast destination address.
sections.eli5: The note on the package says which one is the spare and how long to wait for it. The listener plays whichever arrives first and keeps the other as a backup.

sections.title: Congestion Control
sections.content:
RTP duplication MUST NOT be used where the main cause of loss is congestion, and SHOULD NOT be used where duplicating risks causing congestion. It is RECOMMENDED only to guard against outages from a temporary link or network element failure, where it is known, for example by explicit operator configuration, that there is enough capacity. That limits it to managed networks and makes it unsuitable for unmanaged public networks.

The nodes that duplicate and de-duplicate must know the original stream's requirements and the available capacity, and must assume the same adaptation for the duplicate. If the source doubles the original bitrate, the duplicate's bitrate doubles too.

If de-duplication happens inside the network before the endpoints, the process is transparent and the endpoints apply congestion control to the cleaned stream. If it happens at the endpoint, the endpoint MUST consider the aggregate of both streams in any congestion control it applies. It can also tune the duplication interval from the losses it sees, and the RTP Monitoring Framework can monitor the duplicated streams.
sections.eli5: Never send extra copies when the road is already jammed, because that makes the jam worse. Only do it on roads you know have spare room.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The security considerations of RFC 3550, RFC 7104, RFC 7197 and any RTP profiles and payload formats in use apply. If the original stream is authenticated, for example with SRTP, the duplicate must be authenticated too, and duplicates that fail the check must be discarded.

Middleboxes that duplicate or de-duplicate must rewrite the SSRC of duplicate packets and handle RTCP for the duplicate stream. An in-network duplication service could amplify a denial-of-service attack if an attacker could get attack traffic duplicated, so it must authenticate the traffic it duplicates. This requires the middlebox to be part of the security context and see the session setup signaling and keying material. A de-duplicating middlebox likewise needs to authenticate both streams and not use unauthenticated packets.

SRTP encryption does not affect de-duplication middleboxes, since RTP headers are sent in the clear.
sections.eli5: A helper who makes copies of your messages must check that the messages are really yours. Otherwise a troublemaker could use the helper to flood someone with copies.

data.title: Duplicated video stream
data.code:
m=video 30000 RTP/AVP 100
c=IN IP4 233.252.0.1/127
a=source-filter:incl IN IP4 233.252.0.1 198.51.100.1
a=rtpmap:100 MP2T/90000
a=ssrc:1000 cname:ch1a@example.com
a=ssrc:1010 cname:ch1a@example.com
a=ssrc-group:DUP 1000 1010
a=duplication-delay:50
a=mid:Ch1
